answer_text: Under Article 12(3) GDPR, the controller must respond within one month of receipt of the request, and that period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests.
The prohibitions apply from 2 February 2025, and the Regulation applies in general from 2 August 2026.
At least once every six months, starting by 17 February 2023, and the average is calculated over the period of the past six months.
Without an agreed time or period, the trader must deliver the goods without undue delay and, in any event, not more than 30 days after the day on which the contract is entered into.

No — both fail under the GDPR.

- Recitals of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 state that silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent, so the pre-ticked box is not valid consent [1].
- Article 7(3) GDPR gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw as to give consent [2].
- A signed-letter-only rule makes withdrawal harder than giving consent (a simple click), so it violates Article 7(3) [2].
- Consent must be a clear affirmative action, freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous [1], [6].

Yes — the retailer's use is caught by the prohibition; the university's research use is not.

- The Act prohibits placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems intended to detect the emotional state of individuals in situations related to the workplace and education [1].
- That prohibition only excepts systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, such as therapeutic use — a retail staff-monitoring system does not qualify [1].
- The retailer's use is in a workplace context, so it falls squarely within the prohibition [1].
- The university's system was specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, which is excluded from the Regulation's scope [4][5].
- However, that exclusion is without prejudice to the obligation to comply with the Regulation if the system is later placed on the market or put into service as a result of that research — which is what happens when the retailer deploys it [5].
- The underlying rationale is that emotion inference from biometric data has limited reliability and may lead to discriminatory outcomes and intrude on rights and freedoms [2].

Under Article 20, the platform must give the user access to an internal complaint-handling system to challenge the removal decision. The user can lodge a complaint electronically and free of charge, for a period of at least six months, starting on the day the user is informed of the decision in accordance with Article 16(5) or Article 17. The system must be easy to access, user-friendly, and enable sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated complaints, and the platform must handle complaints in a timely, non-discriminatory, diligent and non-arbitrary manner.

The company had to notify the Commission without delay and in any event within 2 months after the thresholds were met, providing the relevant information identified in Article 3(2) for each core platform service meeting the thresholds (Article 3(3), Digital Markets Act). If it fails to notify and also fails to provide the information requested under Article 21 within the Commission's deadline, the Commission may still designate it as a gatekeeper based on information available to the Commission (Article 3).

Maximum fine for failing to notify: NOT_FOUND

No — the short-term right to reject is no longer available, and the next remedy is the right to repair or replacement.

- Under section 22(3), the time limit for exercising the short-term right to reject is the end of 30 days beginning with the first day after ownership/possession has been transferred, the goods have been delivered, and (where required) the trader has notified the consumer that installation or other enabling action has been taken. Ten weeks have passed, so that limit has expired (section 22(1)).
- Section 19(3) sets out the hierarchy of rights for goods not of satisfactory quality: first the short-term right to reject, then the right to repair or replacement (section 23), then the right to a price reduction or the final right to reject (sections 20 and 24). Having lost the short-term right to reject, the consumer can require the trader to repair or replace the faulty laptop.
- Note that under section 23(6)–(7), a consumer who requires or agrees to a repair or replacement cannot then reject the goods or demand the other remedy without first giving the trader a reasonable time to repair or replace them, unless doing so would cause significant inconvenience.

The provided passages do not address whether the consumer must prove the fault existed at delivery, so no answer can be given on that point from the evidence supplied.

Digital Services Act - threshold: average monthly active recipients of the service in the Union equal to or higher than 45 million (equivalent to 10 % of the Union population), calculated as an average over a period of six months.

Digital Markets Act - threshold: at least 45 million monthly active end users established or located in the Union in the last financial year.

Digital Markets Act - additional requirement: at least 10 000 yearly active business users established in the Union, and the thresholds in point (b) must have been met in each of the last three financial years.

The DSA counts average monthly active recipients of an online platform or search engine service in the Union, while the DMA counts monthly active end users established or located in the Union; alongside the 45 million end users, the DMA also requires at least 10 000 yearly active business users established in the Union, with those thresholds met in each of the last three financial years.

AI Act prohibited AI practice: 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover
Digital Services Act very large online platform: 6 % of total worldwide annual turnover
Digital Markets Act gatekeeper (first offence): 10 % of total worldwide annual turnover

Ranked highest to lowest: Digital Markets Act gatekeeper (10 %), AI Act prohibited practice (7 %), Digital Services Act platform (6 %).

The AI Act uses the GDPR's definition. Article 3(50) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 defines 'personal data' as "personal data as defined in Article 4, point (1), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679". That GDPR definition (Article 4(1)) says personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person ('data subject'), where an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier, or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.

Part 3 (law enforcement), section 35 breach - Data Protection Act 2018: failure to comply with section 35 attracts the higher maximum amount, which per section 157(5) is £17,500,000 (see evidence [5]).
EU company - GDPR basic principles breach: maximum penalty of 20 million Euros (per evidence [5], substituting for £17,500,000 in Article 83(5)/section 157(5)).

The police force faces the higher maximum amount of £17,500,000, while the EU company faces up to 20 million Euros; the two figures are of similar magnitude but denominated in different currencies, so they are not directly comparable without exchange-rate conversion.

GDPR controller - personal data breach notification: not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, where feasible.
AI Act provider - serious incident reporting (general case): not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident.

The GDPR's 72-hour deadline is shorter than the AI Act's 15-day deadline (72 hours vs 15 days).
